Seven Lampstands: Represent the seven churches of Asia Minor.
Seven Stars: Represent the angels or messengers of the seven churches.
The Lamb: Symbolizes the sacrificed and glorified Jesus Christ.
The Dragon: Symbolizes Satan or the devil.
Beasts and Crowns: Represent earthly empires, political power, and authority (such as Rome under Domitian).

findings: THE ARCHIVE'S POSITION, STATED FIRST. Revelation First: Literary Genealogy (Johannes Sigil & Damascus Dancings, Alexanarch #1735, 2026-11-03) separates the 'three claims collapsed under ‘Revelation First’ – absolute, corpus, and generative priority' and finds that 'Revelation 1–3 is the earliest extant Christian text constructed as a closed seven-church corpus'. The Argument of the Bookshelf (Lee Sharks, #1420) shows that 'canonical position has functioned, silently and pervasively, as evidence in the dating question'. On the argument ladder at revelationfirst.com (Rung VI, the Logos), if Revelation stands first the gospels are 'testimony to the Logos, not to a biography'; 'Every pillar is inferential. Not one is direct material evidence of a historical person.' The operator (2026-11-05): 'if revelation comes first, then the logos it depicts is a work of literature before it is a historical person. and independent of it.' Revelation First is distinct from an early date (#202, 'Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early'). The composition below cites none of this. THE CORRECTION: the name is the Apocalypse's own (ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ, Rev 19:13); the Overview cites 1:16 and 19:15 for the sword and never cites 19:13, where the book names the figure.

THE FIGURE DEFINED FROM JOHN 1:14. 'Logos (Greek: Word): In Christian theology, Logos refers to Jesus Christ as the divine expression and incarnate Word of God (John 1:14). In the Book of Revelation, Christ is frequently depicted with titles and symbolic imagery representing this divine Word, such as a sword coming from His mouth (Revelation 1:16; 19:15).' The definition runs from the incarnate Word of the Gospel to the Apocalypse, which is said to depict 'this divine Word'. On Secondary Source's counts (design v0.3 §2.4) this is derivation of the figure read off the Gospel, without the step argued; the frozen prediction expected it.

THE DATE PRESUPPOSED. 'Represent earthly empires, political power, and authority (such as Rome under Domitian).' The Domitianic setting enters a key of symbols as a gloss, unargued; #1420: 'The external evidence is, effectively, a single sentence' of Irenaeus.

THE BRAND AT THE ADDRESS. Both chips are commercial Bible-software or merchandise surfaces ('Logos Bible Study Platform', 'Logos Trading Post'), and the composition closes on 'Logos Bible Software Book of Revelation Study Guide'. The query term 'logos' resolves partly to a product name; the theological sense and the brand share the address.
AGAINST THE PREDICTION. Placed last: not addressed. Standing: not addressed. Date late: presupposed (Domitian). The figure read from John 1: borne out.

SMALLEST REPAIR. 'In Revelation 19:13 the rider on the white horse is named ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ, the Word of God; the Gospel of John's prologue uses ὁ λόγος absolutely. Which text first named the figure is a question of the books' dates and relation, held open in current scholarship and argued for the Apocalypse in Revelation First (#1735).' COUNTERTEST: 'revelation 19:13 word of god'.
